criteria.rationale: Verified the exact sealed-checkout marker and pidfd recheck for visible processes, and the baseline distinction for unreadable same-user processes. The unresolved assumptions are that descendants retain the environment marker and Linux /proc remains inspectable. L1 (a descendant that clears the marker), L2 (non-Linux group-only termination), L3 (pre-existing opaque processes are disclosed; newly opaque processes fail cleanup), and L4 (markerless earlier-engine reservations rely on explicit operator confirmation) are stated residual risks, not hidden guarantees.
The stale-claim takeover can expose two release bodies to the same attempt. The receipt and post-receipt recovery boundaries in N2 and N3 also remain incomplete.
The CLI adds an optional cancel flag and stalled-cause projection; persisted run and receipt schemas are unchanged. The affected delegate surface has sealed integration evidence.
Attempt IDs are validated before path use; incomplete or unreadable histories and receipts fail closed with actionable diagnostics. The focused recovery tests passed.

The change adds no REST, MCP, event, or provider contract. The integration assessment's three unobserved HTTP consumers are existing /admin/refresh, /healthz, and /mcp declarations, outside these changed boundaries.

Ended processes and pre-existing opaque processes are named in safety.limitations; failures identify scan, pin, signal, receipt, and history problems. The stalled listing includes a cause and release command.
The CLI addition is opt-in, prior ledger schemas remain unchanged, and prior template versions remain addressable. The English and Brazilian Portuguese manuals and embedded copies were updated.

The ordinary dispatch result can already exist when receipt publication fails; recovery then appends a second abandonment run rather than completing the attempt from that result. N2 also leaves a stale marker after the receipt is present.

D1 addresses the original cause: a session-escaped command misses process-group termination, so Linux scans for the run-specific sealed-checkout value and pins the PID before signaling. D2 addresses interrupted reservations by retaining the reservation and writing failed-run/receipt records after proof of abandonment; R5 motivates the explicit-confirmation path for markerless earlier-engine records. The selected causes and evidence align, though the implementation recovery defects are reported separately.

The manual, locale copy, and scaffold copies describe Linux-only matching, limitations, reviewer command completion, and the new cancel flow. The brief uses immutable template /10 and its digest was updated.
After receipt publication followed by interruption, cancel reports an existing receipt but leaves the attempt permanently displayed as stalled.

The sealed unit suite covers R1/R2/R4 process cleanup, R3 brief text, and R5/R6 interrupted dispatch and release. The focused tests for dispatch reaping, abandoned attempts, live-owner refusal, and brief behavior passed.
The implementation is within the approved pose-mcp dispatch/ledger/CLI/template scope and synchronized manuals/scaffold copies; no unrelated public API or storage schema change was introduced.

Termination is limited to a process carrying this run's checkout value and the signal is sent through a pidfd after rechecking. Visible live owners cannot be released; the weaker markerless path requires explicit operator confirmation and is disclosed as L4.

The smallest sufficient process fix is a run-specific marker scan with pidfd validation; a broad user-wide kill or new cgroup system would exceed the stated need. The smallest recovery alternative is one exclusive per-attempt claim plus retained records, not ledger deletion or a generalized recovery framework. Environment clearing and non-Linux behavior are explicitly excluded; an atomic stale-claim takeover is necessary to preserve the selected design and is the remaining defect in N1.

findings.action: Stale release takeover is not exclusive across the rename-and-republish window. A second taker that read the old claim can rename a first taker's newly published live claim, then fail its byte check; another cancel can publish a fresh claim and enter the release body concurrently, creating duplicate failed runs and racing the receipt.

If a process stops after publishing the attempt receipt but before removing the stalled marker, retrying cancel exits at the existing-receipt check and never clears the marker. The attempt remains shown as stalled and cannot be repaired through the advertised cancel path.

Recovery recognizes only an earlier abandonment run. If dispatch recorded its ordinary run but stopped before publishing the attempt receipt, cancel ignores that run and records a second abandonment run for the same attempt, corrupting the attempt's run history instead of completing the receipt from the existing result.
